title: \(\mathrm{QMA}(2)\) versus NEXP
formal: Is \(\mathrm{QMA}(2)=\mathrm{NEXP}\) for ordinary promise problems without an oracle? Equivalently, does every promise problem decidable by a nondeterministic classical Turing machine in time \(2^{p(n)}\), for some polynomial \(p\), admit a uniform polynomial-time quantum verifier with two polynomial-length unentangled witnesses, completeness at least \(2/3\), and soundness at most \(1/3\)? The known inclusion \(\mathrm{QMA}(2)\subseteq\mathrm{NEXP}\) makes the reverse containment the unresolved direction. The verifier, its running time and both witness lengths must remain polynomial in the original binary input length.

source_formulation.text: Does ordinary QMA(2), with a constant completeness–soundness gap, equal nondeterministic exponential time?
source_formulation.caption: Editorial paraphrase of Section 1.3, printed page 53:12

why: Two short quantum messages may contain a highly structured encoding of a much longer computation, while their independence restricts how a dishonest prover can cheat. This question asks whether that resource reaches the full power of nondeterministic exponential time despite a polynomial-time verifier and a constant reliability gap. It locates the upper end of the unusually wide known range for QMA(2).
status_note: Source-open for ordinary constant-gap QMA(2) versus NEXP. importance.reason: A major class-comparison problem at the interface of quantum verification, unentanglement and exponential-time complexity. Nearby small-gap and restricted-amplitude models already reach NEXP, but neither supplies the ordinary constant-gap result. It is distinct from, though tightly related to, QMA versus QMA(2).

sentences: The question asks whether polynomial-time verification of two unentangled polynomial-length quantum proofs captures nondeterministic exponential time.
It compares ordinary promise classes with a fixed constant acceptance gap and no oracle or advice.
NEXP already contains QMA(2), so the unresolved direction is verification of every NEXP promise problem by the two-proof model.
Exponentially small-gap and nonnegative-amplitude variants have stronger known characterizations that do not automatically transfer to this model.
Recent amplification and oracle results retain those distinctions and do not establish ordinary QMA(2) equals NEXP.

definitions:
A promise problem is an ordered pair \(L=(L_{\mathrm{yes}},L_{\mathrm{no}})\) of disjoint subsets of \(\{0,1\}^*\). There is no requirement on inputs outside their union. A verifier is specified by one deterministic classical Turing machine that, on a string \(x\) of length \(n\), outputs in time polynomial in \(n\) the description of a quantum circuit \(V_x\), its witness-register lengths and a designated output qubit. All register lengths and the number of gates are bounded by a polynomial depending on the verifier, not on \(x\). Apart from its witness registers, the circuit starts with ancillary qubits in state \(|0\rangle\). It uses the fixed gate set \(\{H,T,\mathrm{CNOT}\}\), acting on specified qubits, where \[H=\frac1{\sqrt2}\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&-1\end{pmatrix},\qquad T=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&e^{i\pi/4}\end{pmatrix},\] and \(\mathrm{CNOT}|a,b\rangle=|a,a\mathbin\oplus b\rangle\) for bits \(a,b\); \(\oplus\) is addition modulo two. The circuit accepts when its final computational-basis measurement of the output qubit is 1. Qubits are two-dimensional complex systems; an \(m\)-qubit pure state is a unit vector in \(\mathbb C^{2^m}\), with computational basis \(\{|z\rangle:z\in\{0,1\}^m\}\). A mixed state is a positive semidefinite, trace-one complex matrix on this space. For witness density matrix \(\rho\), acceptance probability is \[\operatorname{Tr}\!\left[\Pi_1V_x\bigl(\rho\otimes |0\rangle\langle0|^{\otimes a}\bigr)V_x^\dagger\right],\] where \(a\) is the number of ancillary qubits, \(V_x^\dagger\) is the conjugate transpose, and \(\Pi_1\) projects onto output-qubit value 1 and acts as identity on the other qubits. Positive semidefinite means \(v^\dagger\rho v\ge0\) for every vector \(v\); \(\operatorname{Tr}\) is the sum of diagonal entries. Witnesses may depend arbitrarily on the whole input and need not be efficiently preparable. Circuit uniformity forbids advice depending only on input length, and neither model receives an oracle. The witness is sent once, before verification, with no further interaction. The stated finite universal gate set fixes an encoding; bounded-error classes permit the usual polynomial-overhead approximations of other effective universal gate sets. A different verifier and polynomial bound may be used for each promise problem.

The class \(\mathrm{QMA}\), quantum Merlin–Arthur, consists of the promise problems with such a verifier and one polynomial-length quantum witness register for which both conditions hold: for every \(x\in L_{\mathrm{yes}}\), some witness state is accepted with probability at least \(2/3\); for every \(x\in L_{\mathrm{no}}\), every witness state is accepted with probability at most \(1/3\). The quantifiers apply to arbitrary mixed states, not merely the honestly intended state. Pure witnesses suffice for completeness by linearity of acceptance probability.

For \(\mathrm{QMA}(2)\), the verifier instead has two witness registers, each of length bounded by a polynomial in the input length. For every yes-input there must exist density matrices \(\rho\) and \(\sigma\) on the respective registers such that the product state \(\rho\otimes\sigma\) is accepted with probability at least \(2/3\). For every no-input and every pair \(\rho,\sigma\), the acceptance probability on \(\rho\otimes\sigma\) is at most \(1/3\). The two factors can each have arbitrary internal entanglement among their own qubits; the restriction concerns the division between the two registers. Equivalent soundness quantification allows every separable state \(\sum_jp_j\rho_j\otimes\sigma_j\), where \(p_j\ge0\) and \(\sum_jp_j=1\), because acceptance is linear. The two witnesses need not be identical. Both may depend on the whole input and may be coordinated before they are sent, but their joint state at receipt must satisfy the indicated separability restriction. After receipt, the verifier may perform arbitrary allowed joint gates and create entanglement. It is not required to test separability of an arbitrary incoming state; separability is a promise on the states against which soundness is required. Neither class restricts amplitudes to be nonnegative or witness states to have short classical descriptions. Equality means equality of all disjoint promise pairs admitted by the two definitions.

A nondeterministic classical Turing machine has finitely many tapes, a fixed finite tape alphabet and a fixed finite transition relation. An execution chooses one permitted transition at each step, and one step is charged for each such transition. A promise problem \(L=(L_{\mathrm{yes}},L_{\mathrm{no}})\) is in \(\mathrm{NEXP}\), nondeterministic exponential time, if there exist such a machine and an integer-valued polynomial \(p\) with the following properties. Every computation branch on every length-\(n\) binary input halts within \(2^{p(n)}\) steps; every yes-input has an accepting branch; and no no-input has an accepting branch. No correctness requirement is imposed outside the promise. The machine is fixed for the problem and has neither an oracle nor advice. The polynomial and machine may differ between promise problems. Here QMA(2) retains the constant error thresholds already defined. A class allowing an exponentially small difference between completeness and soundness is called a precise variant; that is not the class being compared in this card.
answer_criterion: Provide a complete Lean-checked proof of \(\mathrm{NEXP}\subseteq\mathrm{QMA}(2)\), or a complete Lean-checked proof that a promise problem in NEXP is outside QMA(2). A positive proof must preserve polynomial verification and proof lengths with the fixed \(2/3\) versus \(1/3\) acceptance gap; a negative proof must exclude every ordinary uniform verifier with two unentangled polynomial-length witnesses. A protocol with an exponentially small gap, an exponentially long proof, extra oracle access, or a restriction to nonnegative dishonest witness amplitudes does not by itself satisfy this target. Equality or separation between QMA and QMA(2) alone does not answer their comparison with NEXP.

context_blocks.text: The comparison is about how much computation can be verified, not the physical size of a state vector’s written description. A polynomial number of qubits has exponentially many amplitudes, but an efficient verifier can access them only through its permitted quantum computation. A constant completeness–soundness gap is a substantive part of the claim.

The original source records equality between NEXP and a precise version of QMA(2) whose gap may be exponentially small. Such a verifier may distinguish its yes- and no-cases by a probability difference too small for polynomially many repetitions to resolve. The present card retains the ordinary constant-gap definition.

Known amplification for ordinary QMA(2) and equivalence of two to polynomially many unentangled proofs do not convert every exponentially small-gap protocol into a polynomial-time constant-gap one. The initial gap is a parameter of the amplification cost.

Nonnegative-amplitude proof systems impose additional conditions on the witnesses allowed in the soundness case. Results reaching NEXP in such models therefore concern a different collection of dishonest proofs. The 2024 source explicitly distinguishes those results from ordinary QMA(2).

The August 2026 preprint reports stronger amplification for the nonnegative-amplitude variant, approaching the one-quarter soundness threshold from above as completeness approaches one. Its abstract distinguishes that regime from the stronger-gap comparison with ordinary or real-amplitude witnesses. It does not state the unrestricted equality asked here.

The September 2026 manuscript still records the chain from QMA through QMA(2) to NEXP as the general ordinary-class information available. Its new theorem separates QMA from QMA(2) relative to a unitary oracle; that theorem neither puts all NEXP problems in ordinary QMA(2) nor separates them from it.

The neighboring single-witness question concerns the lower end of the containment chain. This card concerns the upper end. Their logical relationship is worth retaining, but they ask different equalities and a result about one pair does not automatically settle the other.
